newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian shoppers struggle with hyper-inflation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian shoppers struggle with hyper-inflation.

text.p: Bulgarians, trapped in a deepening economic crisis, are struggling to make ends meet as hyper-inflation destroys the value of the lev and sends prices soaring.
"People enter the shop, look at the goods and the prices, and leave," said Iliana Popova, an assistant in a grocery in Sofia's Ovcha Kupel suburb.
"Usually they buy a loaf of bread and some milk and that is all. From time to time somebody buys some sausages," she added.

The lev has fallen below 1,000 to the dollar for the first time -- it was 70 to the dollar a year ago -- and monthly inflation in January is forecast at 50 percent. Economists say annual inflation could top 3,600 percent this year.
The economic crisis is aggravated by a political deadlock and 23 days of protests by students and opposition parties who want the ruling ex-communist Socialist party to hold immediate elections.
Ignoring calls by President Petar Stoyanov for an immediate election, the Socialists accepted a mandate on Tuesday to form a new government and complete their term.
"What are the Socialists trying to do with us? To liquidate the nation?" said Ivelina Yankova while her three-year-old boy screamed for a banana -- which she refused to buy.
The trading centre in Lyulin, a district inhabited by many young families, was deserted because of prices moving ever upwards, salesmen said.
Young people and pensioners around the markets stared at midday meat prices, which were above 1,000 levs -- around $1 -- per kilo.
"Often young people buy only 100 grams of meat. Pensioners are just not among our customers," said Bogdan Dimov, standing idle behind the stand.
Young mothers complained they could not feed their children properly while pensioners said they were forced to sell possessions to pay for bread.
"We are desperate. Quite often I do not sleep because I have two little children and I cannot feed them properly," said 26-year-old Boriana Nedeva.

"How can I buy a chicken when its price today is 855 levs per kilo? All I can spend is 165 levs for bread and another 165 levs for milk because my husband's salary is 15,000 levs (around $15) per month," she said.
With inflation devastating the lev's value, some Bulgarians bought electric appliances as a way to "invest" money, meaning to spend it on something solid before it becomes worthless.

"Middle-aged people are buying cheap lamps and electrical appliances to invest their last savings in goods. Otherwise they will have only paper in their pockets," said Ivan Ivanov, a salesmen in Lyulin's trade centre.
